blocks: It is important to note that this coordinate system is for the far-field where the plane can be considered as a point-mass; consequently, there is no explicit origin for this coordinate system. Each value of θ defines a new set of φ values.

(Note: Throughout the STARS project, φ has been used in this way to define the antenna coordinate system. In the earlier sections of this paper, φ also represented the geodetic latitude, as is the usual custom. The geodetic latitude was subscripted to prevent confusion. The author apologizes for this, but decided not to change the symbols just for this section of the paper.)

Let R′ be the vector from the center of the aircraft to the observation point, e.g. a TDRSS satellite. Drop a perpendicular line segment from R′ onto the x-axis (Figure 5a). Use this location on the x-axis as the origin for a new set of phi angles as defined above (see Figure 5b).
z = z′ cos(φ) = R′ sin(θ) cos(φ)
y = z′ sin(φ) = R′ sin(θ) sin(φ)
The final azimuth and elevation calculations can then be derived. Figure 6a and Figure 6b below show the graphical derivation for the azimuth and elevation calculations, respectively.
tan α = y/x = R′ sin(θ) sin(φ) / R′ cos(θ) = sin(θ) sin(φ) / cos(θ)
tan ε = z / √(x² + y²) = R′ sin(θ) cos(φ) / √(R′² cos²(θ) + R′² sin²(θ) sin²(φ))
